stances.claim: The current US Supreme Court's practices -- undisclosed royalties and gifts, billionaire-funded vacations, hobnobbing in private clubs, and partisan political bias -- represent a fall from the standards CJ revered, turning his lifelong awe into 'dismay' and 'desolation.'

Justice Thomas's late disclosure of Bali and Monte Rio hospitality from Republican mega-donor Harlan Crow as 'inadvertently omitted' -- and his reliance on ethics-official advice that 'personal hospitality from friends need not be disclosed' -- does not absolve the lapse.

Justice Alito's defense that his wife alone hoisted the upside-down flag is undermined by neighbor Emily Baden's CNN interview: the altercation occurred in mid-February (police called Feb. 15, 2021) while the upside-down flag was published Jan. 17, 2021. He is 'at best mistaken, but at worst, he's just lying.'
stances.rhetorical_move: chronology-based credibility audit using a quoted witness

stances.claim: Thomas and Alito should have recused in the pending Jan. 6 and Trump immunity cases; their refusals are 'stubborn' and damaging to institutional legitimacy.
The Scotus code of ethics promulgated late last year has 'no enforcement mechanism' -- interpretation is left to each justice -- which renders it analogous to international law: aspirational at best.

The Philippine Supreme Court, in contrast, penalizes unethical conduct in practice -- two justices fined and disqualified from law practice (one for not reporting filial relationship with a bar examinee, the other for being the source of a premature draft-decision leak), and a chief justice ousted by a close 8-6 vote for failure to file SALN as a law professor before joining the Court.
stances.rhetorical_move: comparative-institutional contrast in favor of the PH SC

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban traces a personal arc from lifelong awe at the US Supreme Court -- whose justices he regarded as 'deities in the legendary Mount Olympus,' quoting Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr., Benjamin Cardozo, and Felix Frankfurter, and admiring Hugo Black, William Brennan, and Thurgood Marshall -- to dismay at current ethical practices. He recalls pilgrimages to the SCOTUS office (visits to Sandra Day O'Connor, Anthony Kennedy, and the deceased Antonin Scalia, and homage at John Marshall's bronze statue), then itemizes the recent financial disclosures: royalties of $340,000 (Brett Kavanaugh), $250,000 (Neil Gorsuch), $87,000 (Sonia Sotomayor), and even new Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson's $900,000 book advance, four Beyoncé tickets worth about $3,700, and $12,500 for chamber artwork, all on top of the 2023 salaries of $285,400 (justices) and $298,500 (chief justice) per www.uscourts.gov. Senior Justice Clarence Thomas only belatedly disclosed Republican mega-donor Harlan Crow's 2019 hospitality in Bali and Monte Rio as 'inadvertently omitted,' explaining that ethics officials advised that 'personal hospitality' from friends need not be disclosed. Worse, Justice Samuel Alito allegedly took a private-jet Alaska vacation with a hedge-fund billionaire with interests before the Court -- undisclosed thanks to a 90-day filing extension. The New York Times photographed an upside-down US flag at Alito's home -- a signal the US Code permits only for 'dire distress or extreme danger,' but in January 2021 widely tied to the stolen-2020-election narrative and the Jan. 6 Capitol riot. Alito blamed his wife Martha Ann's altercation with a neighbor, but neighbor Emily Baden told CNN's Erin Burnett that Alito was 'at best mistaken, but at worst, he's just lying,' since the altercation occurred in mid-February (police call Feb. 15, 2021) while the upside-down flag photograph dates to Jan. 17, 2021. A second NYT photo showed an 'Appeal to Heaven' flag -- a Revolutionary War banner re-adopted by Trump supporters -- at Alito's New Jersey home. Both Thomas and Alito refused to recuse from pending Jan. 6 and Trump-immunity cases ('My wife is fond of flying flags. I am not.'). The Scotus code of ethics promulgated late last year has 'no enforcement mechanism' -- like international law. By contrast, CJ recalls, the Philippine Supreme Court penalizes unethical conduct: two justices fined and disqualified from law practice (one for not reporting a filial relationship with a bar examinee, the other as source of a premature draft-decision leak), and a chief justice ousted 8-6 for failing to file SALN as a law professor before joining the Court.
